meanings.short: The rule that a system moves along the path for which the action, the time total of its Lagrangian, is stationary.
meanings.long: Among all paths between the same starting and end points at the same two times, the real motion is the one for which the action does not change to first order when the path is varied slightly. Often the action is a minimum, hence the old name 'least action', but stationary is what the rule needs. The Euler–Lagrange equations follow from it.

everyday: In everyday speech an action is something done; in mechanics it is a number computed for a whole path of motion.

meanings.short: A number given to a whole path of motion: the Lagrangian added up over time along that path.
meanings.long: The action is the time integral of the Lagrangian from the start to the end of a path. Hamilton's principle says that the real motion makes it stationary. It has the units of energy times time, joule seconds, the same units as Planck's constant.

meanings.short: Working or operation, in the everyday sense: laser action is a laser giving out its strong, orderly light.
A function of a system's coordinates, velocities and time, usually kinetic minus potential energy, from which its equations of motion follow.
meanings.long: For most mechanical systems the Lagrangian is L = T − V, the kinetic energy minus the potential energy. Feeding it into the Euler–Lagrange equations gives the equations of motion, and its time integral is the action. The same idea extends to fields, where a Lagrangian density is integrated over space.

meanings.short: Of a description of a fluid or gas: following each element as it moves, labelled by where it started.
meanings.long: Its advantage is that Newton's laws apply directly to each labelled element; cosmology's comoving coordinates use the same idea for galaxies. The other way, recording what passes each fixed point, is the Eulerian description.

meanings.short: The Lagrangian of a field per unit length, area or volume, which adds up over space to give the whole Lagrangian.
meanings.long: For a field such as the displacement of a stretched rod, the Lagrangian is an integral over space of a density built from the field and its derivatives. The field's equation of motion follows from a version of the Euler–Lagrange equation with derivatives in space as well as time.

meanings.short: The equation a path must satisfy to make an integral such as the action stationary; in mechanics, the equation of motion from a Lagrangian.
meanings.long: For each coordinate q it reads d/dt (∂L/∂q̇) − ∂L/∂q = 0. It comes from the calculus of variations and turns Hamilton's principle into one equation of motion per generalized coordinate.

meanings.short: Any set of numbers, such as angles or distances, that fixes the position of every part of a system.
meanings.long: Generalized coordinates need not be Cartesian: a pendulum is described by one angle, a rigid body by three position coordinates and three angles. When constraints are built in, their number equals the number of degrees of freedom.

meanings.short: The share of the forces that goes with one generalized coordinate: the work done per unit change of that coordinate.
meanings.long: If the coordinate q changes by δq while the others stay fixed, the forces do work Q δq; Q is the generalized force for q. For an angle it is a torque, for a length an ordinary force.

meanings.short: A change from one set of coordinates to another, possibly depending on time, that leaves the Euler–Lagrange equations in the same form.
meanings.long: A point transformation replaces the coordinates q by new ones Q(q, t), with the Lagrangian rewritten in the new variables. Unlike a canonical transformation, it does not mix in the momenta.

origin: Greek holos, whole, and nomos, law.

meanings.short: Of a constraint: one that can be written as an equation between the coordinates and time, so it can be used to remove a coordinate.
meanings.long: A bead on a fixed wire or two masses joined by a rigid rod obey holonomic constraints. Each such equation lowers the number of independent coordinates by one.

meanings.short: Of a constraint: one that cannot be written as an equation between the coordinates alone, such as an inequality or a rule about velocities.
meanings.long: A particle that must stay outside a sphere, or a wheel rolling without slipping on a plane, obeys non-holonomic constraints. They cannot be used to remove coordinates and need other methods, such as Lagrange multipliers.

meanings.short: Of a constraint: a linear relation between small changes of the coordinates and time, which may not add up to an equation between the coordinates.
meanings.long: A semi-holonomic constraint has the form Σ a_j(q) dq_j + a_t(q) dt = 0. Rolling without slipping is the standard example. Such constraints can be handled with Lagrange multipliers.

meanings.short: The rule that constraint forces do no work in any small displacement the constraints allow, which gives the equations of motion without them.
meanings.long: It states that the applied forces minus mass times acceleration do no total work in any virtual displacement. Written in generalized coordinates it gives the Euler–Lagrange equations, so it can serve instead of Hamilton's principle as the starting point of mechanics.

meanings.short: A function of the velocities whose derivatives give friction forces that grow in proportion to speed, used to add such friction to Lagrange's equations.
meanings.long: For drag proportional to velocity the dissipation function is half the drag coefficient times the speed squared, summed over particles. Its derivative with respect to each generalized velocity gives the friction force that enters the equation of motion, and twice its value is the rate at which energy is lost.

meanings.short: A potential energy that depends on velocities as well as positions, so that a force such as the magnetic force still fits into a Lagrangian.
meanings.long: If a generalized force can be written as −∂V/∂q + d/dt(∂V/∂q̇) for some V(q, q̇, t), the Lagrangian L = T − V still gives the right equations of motion. The force on a charge in a magnetic field is the main example.

meanings.short: The result that every continuous symmetry of a system's Lagrangian goes with a conserved quantity.
meanings.long: Shifting in time gives conservation of energy, shifting in space conservation of momentum, and turning about an axis conservation of angular momentum. Emmy Noether proved the general theorem in 1918.

meanings.short: The momentum that goes with a coordinate: how fast the Lagrangian changes when that coordinate's velocity changes.
meanings.long: It is defined as p = ∂L/∂q̇. For a free particle in Cartesian coordinates it is the ordinary momentum; for an angle it is an angular momentum; for a charge in a magnetic field it includes a term from the vector potential. If the coordinate does not appear in the Lagrangian, its canonical momentum is conserved.

meanings.short: The energy of a system written as a function of its coordinates and momenta; in quantum mechanics, the operator for that energy.
meanings.long: The Hamiltonian H(q, p, t) is built from the Lagrangian by a Legendre transformation, H = Σ p q̇ − L. For most systems it equals the total energy. Hamilton's equations, or in quantum mechanics the Schrödinger equation, use it to give the motion.

meanings.short: A way of swapping a variable of a function for the slope of the function with respect to it, without losing information.
meanings.long: In mechanics it turns the Lagrangian, a function of velocities, into the Hamiltonian, a function of momenta: H = Σ p q̇ − L with p = ∂L/∂q̇. In thermodynamics the same trick turns energy into enthalpy or free energy.

meanings.short: The equations of motion written as first-order equations for coordinates and momenta: each rate of change is a derivative of the Hamiltonian.
meanings.long: They read q̇ = ∂H/∂p and ṗ = −∂H/∂q for each pair of coordinate and momentum. They replace n second-order Euler–Lagrange equations by 2n first-order ones, and describe the motion as a flow through phase space.

meanings.short: The space of all possible states of a system, one axis for each coordinate and one for each momentum.
meanings.long: A single point of phase space fixes the state completely, positions and momenta together, and as time passes the point traces a trajectory. For one particle in one dimension it is a plane with position across and momentum up. In statistical physics a gas of N particles has a 6N-dimensional phase space.

meanings.short: The space of all possible positions of a system, one axis for each generalized coordinate, with no momenta.
meanings.long: A point of configuration space fixes where every part of the system is but not how fast it moves. Its dimension is the number of degrees of freedom; phase space has twice as many.

meanings.short: One of the independent ways a system can move, counted by the number of coordinates needed to fix its position.
meanings.long: A particle moving in space has three degrees of freedom; a rigid body has six, three for its position and three for its orientation. Each holonomic constraint removes one. In thermal physics the term also counts the independent ways a molecule can store energy.

meanings.short: A way of combining two quantities in phase space, built from their derivatives, that gives rates of change and tests changes of variables.
meanings.long: For quantities u and v, {u, v} = Σ (∂u/∂q ∂v/∂p − ∂u/∂p ∂v/∂q). The rate of change of any u is {u, H} plus its explicit time derivative, so u is conserved when its bracket with the Hamiltonian vanishes. In quantum mechanics the commutator divided by iħ takes its place.

meanings.short: Of a change of phase-space variables: keeping the special structure that pairs each coordinate with its momentum, as canonical transformations do.
meanings.long: The symplectic condition says that the matrix of derivatives M of the new variables with respect to the old satisfies M J Mᵀ = J, where J is a fixed matrix that pairs coordinates with momenta. A transformation is canonical exactly when it meets this condition, and every such transformation keeps phase-space volumes.

meanings.short: A change of coordinates and momenta together that keeps Hamilton's equations in the same form, with a new Hamiltonian.
meanings.long: Canonical transformations mix coordinates and momenta freely, so they are far more flexible than point transformations. They can be built from a generating function, and the best ones make the new Hamiltonian so simple that the motion can be read off. A restricted canonical transformation has no explicit time dependence.

meanings.short: A single function that packs a whole family of things into one expression, so that expanding or differentiating it produces them.
meanings.long: Expanding a generating function as a power series gives a sequence of numbers or functions as its coefficients; the Legendre polynomials, for example, come from one simple expression.

meanings.short: A function of old and new variables whose partial derivatives give a change of variables that is sure to be canonical.
meanings.long: There are four types, F₁(q, Q, t) to F₄(p, P, t), mixing one old and one new set of variables. The new Hamiltonian is the old one plus the generating function's partial derivative with respect to time.

meanings.short: The result that under Hamilton's equations a region of phase space keeps its volume as it moves, though its shape may change.
meanings.long: A cloud of starting states flows through phase space like an incompressible fluid. Because the motion itself is a canonical transformation, the volume cannot grow or shrink. Systems with friction break the rule; their phase-space volumes shrink.

meanings.short: The result that if two quantities are conserved, so is their Poisson bracket.
meanings.long: Sometimes the bracket of two known conserved quantities is a new one; often it is just a combination of those already known. It follows from a property of Poisson brackets called the Jacobi identity.

meanings.short: A single partial differential equation for a function whose solution gives a change of variables in which nothing moves, solving the mechanics problem.
meanings.long: It asks for a generating function S(q, α, t) with H(q, ∂S/∂q, t) + ∂S/∂t = 0. Its solution, Hamilton's principal function, makes all the new coordinates and momenta constant, and the motion follows by differentiating S. When the Hamiltonian does not depend on time it reduces to an equation for the characteristic function W.

meanings.short: The solution S of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation, a generating function that turns the motion into constants; along the real path it equals the action.
meanings.long: S depends on the coordinates, on n constants and on time. Its derivatives with respect to the constants give further constants, from which the coordinates can be found as functions of time. Its total rate of change along the motion is the Lagrangian.

meanings.short: The time-free part W of Hamilton's principal function, used when the energy is conserved: S = W − Et.
meanings.long: W(q, α) is the sum of the integrals of the momenta along the coordinates. It obeys the time-independent Hamilton–Jacobi equation, and it is the generating function from which action-angle variables are built.

meanings.short: Canonical variables for a periodic motion in which the momenta are constant actions and the coordinates are angles that grow steadily in time.
meanings.long: Each action J is the area enclosed by the orbit in phase space (some texts divide by 2π); its partner angle advances at a fixed rate, the frequency of that motion. They give frequencies without solving the motion in detail and are the natural starting point for perturbation theory.

meanings.short: A constant of a periodic motion: the area its orbit encloses in phase space.
meanings.long: It is defined in these notes as J = ∮ p dq around one cycle; many texts divide by 2π. The energy can be written as a function of the actions alone, and the frequencies are the derivatives of the energy with respect to them.

meanings.short: The coordinate that goes with an action variable: it grows at a steady rate and advances by a fixed amount each cycle.
meanings.long: It is the derivative of the characteristic function with respect to the action. Over one full cycle it advances by 1 in these notes (by 2π in texts that divide the action by 2π), and its rate is the frequency of the motion.

origin: Latin librare, to swing like a balance.

meanings.short: A back-and-forth swing in which coordinate and momentum both repeat, so the orbit in phase space is a closed loop.
meanings.long: A pendulum that does not reach the top librates. The other kind of periodic motion is a rotation, in which the coordinate keeps increasing, like a pendulum going over the top again and again.

meanings.short: A curve in phase space that divides orbits of one kind from orbits of another, such as swinging from going over the top.
meanings.long: For a pendulum it is the orbit with just enough energy to reach the top. Motion exactly on a separatrix takes forever to complete, so its period is infinite.

meanings.short: Of a motion: made of several periodic motions with their own frequencies, so it may never repeat as a whole.
meanings.long: Each coordinate oscillates on its own schedule. If the frequencies are in a whole-number ratio, the motion closes and repeats; otherwise the state never quite returns.

meanings.short: The numbers that fix an orbit's size, shape and orientation in space, such as its semi-major axis, eccentricity and tilt.
meanings.long: A Kepler ellipse needs five: inclination and longitude of the ascending node fix its plane; semi-major axis, eccentricity and argument of the pericentre fix the ellipse within the plane. A sixth number says where the body is on it.

everyday: In everyday speech an inclination is a tendency or liking; here it is an angle.

meanings.short: The tilt of an orbit's plane against a chosen reference plane.
meanings.long: An inclination of zero means the orbit lies in the reference plane; 90 degrees means it passes over the poles. It is one of the five orbital elements.

meanings.short: The angle, measured in the reference plane, from a fixed direction to the point where an orbit crosses that plane going upwards.
meanings.long: Together with the inclination it fixes the orbit's plane in space. The point where the orbit rises through the reference plane is the ascending node.

meanings.short: The angle within an orbit's plane from the ascending node to the point of closest approach, which fixes how the ellipse is turned.
meanings.long: A slow change of this angle is a precession of the orbit, such as the precession of Mercury's perihelion.

meanings.short: Half the longest width of an ellipse; for an orbit, the average of its closest and farthest distances from the centre of attraction.
meanings.long: It sets the size of an elliptical orbit, and by Kepler's third law the square of the period is proportional to its cube. In the Kepler problem the energy depends on it alone: E = −k/2a.

meanings.short: A number that says how stretched an orbit or ellipse is: 0 for a circle, between 0 and 1 for an ellipse.
meanings.long: It is the distance from the centre of an ellipse to a focus, divided by the semi-major axis. An eccentricity of exactly 1 gives a parabola and more than 1 a hyperbola, the paths of unbound bodies.

meanings.short: A method of approximation: solve a simpler problem exactly, then add the effect of a small extra term as a series of corrections.
meanings.long: The small term, the perturbation, is measured by a small number, and corrections are found in its first power, then its second, and so on. In classical mechanics it is used to find how a planet's orbit slowly changes; in quantum mechanics how energy levels shift.

origin: Latin saeculum, an age or a century.
everyday: In everyday speech secular means not religious; in physics it means slowly building up over long times.

meanings.short: Of an effect of a perturbation: growing steadily over many cycles instead of averaging out, like the slow turning of an orbit.
meanings.long: A perturbation causes small wobbles that repeat every cycle (periodic effects) and changes that keep adding up (secular effects). Averaging over one period removes the first and leaves the second, which often shows up as a shift of a frequency or a precession.

meanings.short: The motion of a body attracted towards a fixed centre by an inverse-square force, such as a planet round the Sun.
meanings.long: Bound orbits are ellipses with the centre of attraction at one focus. It is one of the few problems in mechanics that can be solved exactly, and its hidden symmetry makes every bound orbit close.

meanings.short: The potential energy plus a term from the angular motion, which turns an orbit into a one-dimensional problem in the distance alone.
meanings.long: For a central force, V_eff(r) = V(r) + ℓ²/2mr², with ℓ the conserved angular momentum. The extra term acts as a barrier at small distances. Where the energy equals V_eff the body turns round in r; a minimum of V_eff gives a circular orbit.

meanings.short: The slow turning of an orbit's long axis, so that the point of closest approach moves round a little each orbit.
meanings.long: Pulls from other planets cause most of Mercury's, but about 43 arcseconds per century are left over, and general relativity explains them exactly. It was the first success of Einstein's theory.

meanings.short: The result that any change of a rigid body's orientation, with one point held fixed, is a single rotation about one axis.
meanings.long: It follows because every rotation matrix has an eigenvalue equal to 1, whose eigenvector is the axis. It is why a body's turning at each instant can be described by one angular velocity vector.

meanings.short: For a function homogeneous of degree k: each variable times the partial derivative with respect to it, summed, gives k times the function.
meanings.long: Applied to kinetic energy, which is homogeneous of degree 2 in the velocities, it gives Σ q̇ ∂T/∂q̇ = 2T, and so shows that the Hamiltonian equals the energy.

meanings.short: Three angles that fix how a rigid body is turned, built from three turns made one after another about chosen axes.
meanings.long: In the usual choice the body is turned by φ about the vertical, then by θ about the new x axis (the line of nodes), then by ψ about its own new z axis. For a spinning top φ is the precession angle, θ the tilt and ψ the spin.

meanings.short: The line where two planes cross: a body's own equator and the fixed horizontal plane, or an orbit and its reference plane.
meanings.long: In the Euler angles it is the axis of the second turn, by the tilt angle θ. For a top, gravity's torque points along it; for an orbit, it joins the ascending and descending nodes.

meanings.short: A set of axes fixed in a rigid body and turning with it.
meanings.long: In the body frame the moment of inertia tensor never changes, which is why Euler's equations are written there. The price is that the frame rotates, so time derivatives pick up extra terms.

meanings.short: A 3 by 3 table of numbers describing how a body's mass is spread round a point; it turns angular velocity into angular momentum.
meanings.long: Its diagonal entries are the moments of inertia about the three axes, the others are the products of inertia. Angular momentum is the tensor times the angular velocity, so in general the two vectors point in different directions. The table is symmetric, so in principal axes it becomes diagonal.

meanings.short: The natural perpendicular axes of a body, or of an ellipse or ellipsoid, along which the matrix that describes it becomes diagonal.
meanings.long: For a rigid body they are the three perpendicular directions about which it can spin with its angular momentum along its angular velocity. They are the eigenvectors of the moment of inertia tensor, and symmetry often shows where they are.

meanings.short: A body's moments of inertia about its three principal axes: the eigenvalues of its moment of inertia tensor.
meanings.long: Rotation about the axes of largest and smallest principal moment is stable; rotation about the intermediate one is not, as a tossed book or phone shows.

meanings.short: The off-diagonal entries of the moment of inertia tensor, such as minus the sum of mass times x times y.
meanings.long: They measure how lopsided a body's mass is with respect to the chosen axes. They all vanish when the axes are principal axes.

meanings.short: The rule that a moment of inertia about any axis equals that about a parallel axis through the centre of mass, plus mass times distance².
meanings.long: It means moments of inertia need only be worked out about the centre of mass. The same idea gives the whole moment of inertia tensor about any point from the one about the centre of mass.

meanings.short: The set of all rotations, written as orthogonal matrices with determinant +1; in three dimensions it is called SO(3).
meanings.long: Orthogonal matrices keep lengths and angles. Those with determinant −1 also include a reflection; leaving them out leaves the pure rotations, which can be combined and undone and so form a group.

meanings.short: Three equations for how a rigid body's spin about its principal axes changes under a torque, written in axes turning with the body.
meanings.long: For the first axis, I₁ω̇₁ − (I₂ − I₃)ω₂ω₃ = τ₁, and the others follow by cycling the labels. With no torque they show that spin about the axis of middle moment is unstable.

meanings.short: Newton's second law for a fluid without viscosity: an element speeds up because of pressure differences and external forces.
meanings.long: It reads ∂v/∂t + (v · ∇)v = −∇P/ρ + f/ρ. The second term, the advective term, makes it nonlinear. Adding viscosity turns it into the Navier–Stokes equation.

meanings.short: One of Euler's three equations for a turning rigid body, each linking the change of spin about one principal axis to the torque.
A spinning body with two equal principal moments of inertia, such as a spinning top, whose third principal axis is its axis of symmetry.
meanings.long: With one point fixed and gravity acting, its axis precesses round the vertical and nods up and down (nutation). Its motion can be solved exactly because two momenta and the energy are conserved.

meanings.short: A slow turning of an axis or an orbit around another direction, as a spinning top's axis sweeps round the vertical.
meanings.long: A torque on a spinning body changes the direction of its angular momentum rather than toppling it, so the spin axis goes round in a cone. Orbits can precess too: their long axis turns slowly, as Mercury's does.

meanings.short: The nodding of a spinning top's axis up and down while it precesses.
meanings.long: The tilt angle of the axis swings between two turning points. Depending on how the top is started, the tip of its axis traces waves, loops or cusps.

meanings.short: The cone traced by the angular velocity around a free symmetric body's axis, seen from the body.
meanings.long: It rolls without slipping on the space cone, and the line where they touch is the instantaneous axis of rotation.

meanings.short: The cone traced by the angular velocity around the fixed angular momentum of a free spinning body, seen from outside.
meanings.long: The body cone rolls on it without slipping, which gives a picture of torque-free precession.

meanings.short: A set of axes that turns relative to the distant stars, such as axes fixed to the spinning Earth.
meanings.long: Because the axes turn, the rate of change of any vector seen in the frame differs from the rate in an inertial frame by ω × the vector. Newton's laws then need fictitious forces: centrifugal, Coriolis and, if the turning changes speed, a third one.

meanings.short: A fictitious force in a rotating frame that pushes a moving body sideways, at right angles to its motion.
meanings.long: It equals −2m ω × v, with v the velocity in the rotating frame, so it acts only on things that move and never changes their speed. On Earth it turns winds to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern.

origin: Latin centrum, centre, and fugere, to flee.

meanings.short: The outward fictitious force felt in a rotating frame, pushing everything away from the axis of rotation.
meanings.long: It equals −m ω × (ω × r): its size is m ω² times the distance from the axis. It acts on everything in the rotating frame, moving or not, and is why the Earth bulges at the equator.

meanings.short: A long pendulum free to swing in any direction, whose plane of swing slowly turns because the Earth rotates beneath it.
meanings.long: The Coriolis force turns the plane of swing at the Earth's rotation rate times the sine of the latitude: a full turn in a day at the poles, none at the equator. Léon Foucault showed it in Paris in 1851.

everyday: Normal here does not mean usual or typical: a normal mode is one of a system's own natural patterns of vibration.

meanings.short: A pattern of motion in which every part of a vibrating system moves at the same frequency, all in step.
meanings.long: A system of coupled oscillators has as many normal modes as degrees of freedom, each with its own frequency. Any small motion is a sum of normal modes. In matrix language they are eigenvectors, and their squared frequencies the eigenvalues.

meanings.short: Coordinates, one for each normal mode, in which a set of coupled oscillators becomes a set of separate, uncoupled ones.
meanings.long: They are found by diagonalising the kinetic and potential energy matrices at the same time. Each normal coordinate then oscillates on its own at its mode's frequency.

meanings.short: A state of a system that does not change: where all rates of change are zero, or, for a map, a point sent to itself.
meanings.long: Near a fixed point the motion can usually be found by linearizing. The eigenvalues of the linearized equations sort fixed points into nodes, saddles, spirals and centres.
meanings.here: Elsewhere on the site a fixed point is usually just a point held still, such as the pivot of a top.

meanings.short: Replacing equations by their straight-line approximation near a point, keeping only terms of first order in the small changes.
meanings.long: Near a fixed point, small departures obey linear equations whose matrix is the Jacobian. Their solutions show whether nearby motion grows, dies away or circles, though borderline cases need the nonlinear terms.

meanings.short: Of a fixed point: every motion that starts close enough to it stays close for all time, though it need not approach it.
meanings.long: A centre is Lyapunov stable but not attracting; nearby orbits circle it forever. A fixed point that is both Lyapunov stable and attracting is called stable.

meanings.short: The set of starting points whose motion flows into a fixed point, such as the line along which paths come in to a saddle.
meanings.long: For a saddle in two dimensions it is a curve; trajectories that start on it reach the saddle, all others are eventually pushed away.

meanings.short: The set of points whose motion, run backwards in time, flows into a fixed point: the paths that leave it.
meanings.long: For a saddle in two dimensions it is the curve along which trajectories depart. Nearby motion is squeezed towards it.

meanings.short: A fixed point that nearby paths approach by spiralling in, as a damped pendulum settles at the bottom.
meanings.long: The linearized equations have complex eigenvalues with negative real part. The same thing is called a spiral sink in some courses.

meanings.short: A fixed point that nearby paths leave by spiralling outwards, as an oscillation whose size keeps growing.
meanings.long: The linearized equations have complex eigenvalues with positive real part. It is also called a spiral source.

meanings.short: A sudden change in the kind of behaviour of a system as a setting is varied smoothly, such as fixed points appearing or vanishing.
meanings.long: At the critical value of the setting, fixed points or cycles are created, destroyed or change their stability. Standard types include the saddle-node, transcritical, pitchfork and Hopf bifurcations.

meanings.short: A graph of where a system settles, its fixed points or cycles, against the setting being varied, with stable and unstable branches marked.
meanings.long: For the logistic map it shows period doublings crowding together and then chaos, with windows of order inside.

meanings.short: A bifurcation in which two fixed points, one stable and one unstable, move together, merge and vanish as a setting is changed.
meanings.long: Just past it the motion slows down where the fixed points used to be, a bottleneck, before moving on. In two dimensions the merging points are a saddle and a node, which gives the name.

meanings.short: A bifurcation in which two fixed points pass through each other and swap their stability.
meanings.long: It happens when a fixed point must always exist, as zero population or zero laser light does. Past the critical value the other fixed point takes over as the stable one, as at a laser's threshold.

meanings.short: A bifurcation in a symmetric system where one fixed point splits into three, drawn like a pitchfork, or three merge into one.
meanings.long: It happens where a symmetry forces fixed points to come in mirror pairs, as for a bead on a spinning hoop. In the supercritical kind the middle point loses stability to two new stable ones; in the subcritical kind unstable ones close in.

meanings.short: A gentle bifurcation: past the critical value, new stable states grow smoothly from zero, so the change is small at first and reversible.
meanings.long: In a supercritical pitchfork two stable fixed points branch off the old one; in a supercritical Hopf a small stable limit cycle grows round it.

meanings.short: A sudden bifurcation: the stable state is lost when unstable states close in on it, so the system jumps far away.
meanings.long: Turning the setting back does not always undo the jump, so the system can show hysteresis. Subcritical pitchfork and Hopf bifurcations are the dangerous kinds in engineering.

meanings.short: A bifurcation in which a fixed point loses stability as a pair of complex eigenvalues crosses into growth, and a limit cycle appears or vanishes.
meanings.long: A steady state turns into a steady oscillation. In the supercritical case a small stable cycle grows from the point; in the subcritical case an unstable cycle shrinks onto it.

origin: Greek homos, same, and klinein, to lean.

meanings.short: A bifurcation in which a limit cycle grows until it touches a saddle point and is destroyed.
meanings.long: At the critical value the cycle becomes a loop that leaves the saddle and comes back to it. Its period grows without limit as that moment approaches.

meanings.short: A bifurcation in which fixed points appear on a limit cycle, so the period of the cycle grows without limit and the oscillation stops.
meanings.long: A driven pendulum shows it: with a large torque it keeps going over the top; as the torque is lowered, the motion near the top slows until a stable rest angle appears.

meanings.short: The result that in two dimensions a path trapped in a region with no fixed points must approach a closed orbit.
meanings.long: It means a flow in the plane can settle only to fixed points, closed orbits or loops joining fixed points. Chaos is impossible there; it needs at least three variables.

meanings.short: An oscillator whose damping is negative for small swings and positive for large ones, so every motion settles onto the same limit cycle.
meanings.long: It was first studied for valve radio circuits in the 1920s. Small oscillations grow and large ones shrink, so all motions end on one cycle of fixed size.

everyday: In everyday speech chaos means complete disorder; in physics a chaotic system follows exact rules, but its future cannot be predicted in practice.

meanings.short: Long-term behaviour of a system with exact rules that never settles or repeats and depends sensitively on where it starts.
meanings.long: Two chaotic motions that start very close separate exponentially fast, so tiny uncertainties grow until prediction fails. Differential equations need at least three variables for chaos; maps can show it in one.

meanings.short: Random and irregular from place to place; here, starting values of a field that differ at random across space.
Of a system: its rules fix its whole future exactly once its present state is known, with no chance involved.
meanings.long: Classical mechanics is deterministic: given the starting conditions, the equations have exactly one solution. Chaos shows that a deterministic system can still be unpredictable in practice.

meanings.short: The property that two motions starting very close together soon become completely different, the mark of chaos.
meanings.long: The distance between them grows roughly exponentially, at a rate set by the largest Lyapunov exponent. It is often called the butterfly effect.

meanings.short: Never settling into a repeating pattern, nor coming to rest.
meanings.long: A chaotic trajectory is aperiodic: it neither approaches a fixed point nor a periodic orbit, but wanders irregularly for ever.

meanings.short: The property that any small region of starting states is stretched by the motion until it overlaps every other region.
meanings.long: It means a chaotic trajectory roams over much of the space available to it, like a drop of dye stirred through a whole glass of water.

meanings.short: A state or set of states that nearby motions approach and then stay near, such as a resting point or a steady cycle.
meanings.long: Only systems that lose energy, or otherwise shrink phase-space volumes, have attractors. The simplest are stable fixed points and stable limit cycles; chaotic systems can have strange attractors.

meanings.short: The set of all starting states whose motion ends up at a given attractor.
meanings.long: A damped pendulum has a basin for each resting position; in a chaotic system the borders between basins can be fractal.

meanings.short: An attractor on which the motion is chaotic, shaped like a fractal with a dimension that is not a whole number.
meanings.long: Nearby motions on it separate quickly, yet all stay on it, because the flow keeps stretching and folding. The Lorenz attractor is the best-known example.

meanings.short: Losing energy, or of the loss of energy, usually as heat, through friction, viscosity or radiation.
meanings.long: In a dissipative system volumes of phase space shrink as time goes on, which is why such systems can settle onto attractors. In a fluid, viscosity dissipates the energy of motion into heat.

meanings.short: A picture of a motion made by marking its state only at regular moments, or each time it crosses a chosen surface.
meanings.long: A periodic motion leaves a few points; a chaotic one fills out an intricate pattern. Sampling turns a flow into a map from one crossing to the next.

meanings.short: The average rate at which two nearby motions separate: their distance grows like e raised to the exponent times time.
meanings.long: A positive largest Lyapunov exponent is the signal of chaos. A system has one exponent per direction; for a dissipative one they add up to a negative number.

meanings.short: The rule x → r x (1 − x), applied again and again, the simplest system that shows period doubling and chaos.
meanings.long: For small r the values settle to a fixed point; as r grows they cycle between 2, then 4, then 8 values, and beyond about 3.57 they become chaotic, with windows of order.

meanings.short: A bifurcation in which a cycle is replaced by one that takes twice as long to repeat.
meanings.long: Repeated period doublings, coming faster and faster, are a common road to chaos. The ratio of the gaps between them tends to Feigenbaum's number.

meanings.short: The number 4.669…, the ratio by which the gaps between successive period doublings shrink, the same for a wide class of systems.
meanings.long: Mitchell Feigenbaum found in 1975 that it does not depend on the details of the map, only on the shape of its maximum. That sameness is called universality.

meanings.short: Containing smaller copies of itself, so that a magnified piece looks like the whole.
meanings.long: Fractals such as the Cantor set and the Koch curve are exactly self-similar. The bifurcation diagram of the logistic map repeats its pattern in miniature.

meanings.short: A shape with fine detail at every scale, whose dimension is usually not a whole number.
meanings.long: Fractals are often self-similar. The Cantor set and the Koch curve are classic examples; strange attractors and coastlines are fractals found in nature.

meanings.short: A measure of how a shape fills space: how fast the number of small boxes needed to cover it grows as the boxes shrink.
meanings.long: If N boxes of size ε are needed and N grows like ε to the power −d, then d is the dimension. A line gives 1 and a square 2; the Cantor set gives about 0.63 and the Koch curve about 1.26.

meanings.short: The fractal left by removing the middle third of a line segment, then the middle third of each remaining piece, and so on for ever.
meanings.long: It has zero total length yet infinitely many points. Its fractal dimension is log 2 / log 3, about 0.63.

meanings.short: The fractal made by replacing the middle third of each line segment with two sides of a triangle, again and again.
meanings.long: Its length grows by a factor 4/3 each step, so it is infinitely long though it fits in a small region. Its fractal dimension is log 4 / log 3, about 1.26.

meanings.short: Three simple equations for convection in a heated fluid, found by Edward Lorenz in 1963 to be chaotic.
meanings.long: Their solutions settle onto a butterfly-shaped strange attractor of fractal dimension about 2.06. Lorenz's discovery that tiny rounding changes gave completely different forecasts made chaos famous.

meanings.short: A formula that estimates the fractal dimension of a strange attractor from its Lyapunov exponents.
meanings.long: For a map in two dimensions with exponents λ₁ > 0 > λ₂ it gives d = 1 + λ₁/|λ₂|. It balances stretching in one direction against squeezing in the other.

meanings.short: Irregular, swirling fluid flow with eddies of many sizes, the opposite of smooth laminar flow.
meanings.long: It sets in when the Reynolds number is large, so inertia overwhelms viscosity. Energy fed into large eddies passes down to smaller and smaller ones until viscosity turns it into heat.

meanings.short: The rule that in strong turbulence the energy in eddies of wavenumber k falls as k to the power −5/3.
meanings.long: Andrey Kolmogorov found it in 1941 by dimensional analysis, assuming that in the inertial range only the rate of energy flow matters. It agrees well with measurements.

meanings.short: In turbulence, the range of eddy sizes much smaller than the largest and much larger than the smallest, where energy only passes through.
meanings.long: There viscosity plays no part and energy simply cascades from larger eddies to smaller ones. Kolmogorov's law describes the energy spectrum in this range.

meanings.short: A swirl of fluid turning round on itself, such as the whirls behind a rock in a stream.
meanings.long: In turbulence, eddies of many sizes form and break up into smaller ones, passing energy down until viscosity turns it into heat.

meanings.short: A tiny piece of fluid, small enough to treat as a point but large enough to contain very many molecules.
meanings.long: Fluid equations follow fluid elements as they move, stretch and change density, applying Newton's laws to each.

meanings.short: A quantity with a value at every point of space and time, treated by ordinary, non-quantum mechanics.
meanings.long: A field can be thought of as a system with infinitely many coordinates, one for each point. Its equations of motion follow from a Lagrangian density, as for a vibrating string or a fluid.

meanings.short: Describing a fluid by recording, at each fixed point of space, the velocity, density and pressure of whatever fluid passes.
meanings.long: The state of the fluid is then a set of fields such as v(r, t), ρ(r, t) and P(r, t). Rates of change seen by a moving element need the total derivative, ∂/∂t + v · ∇.

meanings.short: The rate of change of a function of several variables with respect to one of them, while all the others are held fixed.
meanings.long: It is written with a curly ∂, as ∂f/∂x. In a fluid ∂/∂t is the rate of change at a fixed point, unlike the total derivative, which follows the moving fluid.

meanings.short: The rate of change of a quantity along the actual motion, counting both its change in time and the change from moving to new places.
meanings.long: In a fluid it is d/dt = ∂/∂t + v · ∇: the rate seen by an element carried along by the flow. For a function of coordinates and time it is the derivative along the actual motion.

meanings.short: An expression that is exactly the time or other derivative of one single function, so it can be integrated at once.
meanings.long: Adding a total time derivative dF/dt to a Lagrangian changes the action only by end-point values, so the equations of motion stay the same. A total derivative inside an integral over all values gives just the boundary terms.

meanings.short: Having to do with something being carried along by a moving fluid.
meanings.long: The advective term (v · ∇)v in the Euler equation appears because a fluid element moves to places where the velocity is different. It makes fluid equations nonlinear.

meanings.short: An equation saying that something such as mass or charge is conserved: it changes in a region only by flowing across the edge.
meanings.long: For a fluid it reads ∂ρ/∂t + ∇ · (ρv) = 0. The same form holds for electric charge, with charge density and current density, and for any conserved quantity.

meanings.short: The mass flowing through a unit area each second, density times velocity, pointing along the flow.
meanings.long: Its divergence is how fast mass leaves a point, so by the continuity equation it equals minus the rate at which density falls there.

meanings.short: How much momentum crosses a unit area each second, a tensor since each direction of momentum can flow in each direction.
meanings.long: For an ideal fluid it is P δᵢⱼ + ρ vᵢ vⱼ: pressure plus momentum carried along by the flow. In relativity it is the space-space part of the stress-energy tensor.

meanings.short: The momentum per unit volume of a fluid or field: for a fluid, its density times its velocity.
meanings.long: For a fluid the momentum density ρv also equals the mass flux density. For an electromagnetic field it is the Poynting vector divided by c².

meanings.short: The force per unit volume acting on a fluid or other continuous body.
meanings.long: Gravity, for example, gives a force density ρg. Pressure acts through its gradient, which is itself a force density.

meanings.short: Of a flow: without any local spinning, so the curl of its velocity, the vorticity, is zero everywhere.
meanings.long: An irrotational velocity field can be written as the gradient of a velocity potential. A flow can go round in a circle and still be irrotational, as long as small elements do not spin.

meanings.short: A fluid with no viscosity and no heat flow, whose only internal force is pressure.
meanings.long: Its motion obeys the Euler equation. It is a good model for many flows away from walls, but fails near surfaces, where real fluids form boundary layers.

meanings.short: A 3 by 3 table that gives the force per unit area across a surface facing any direction inside a material or fluid.
meanings.long: Its diagonal entries are pushes or pulls straight across a surface, such as pressure; the others are shear stresses along it. For a fluid it also counts momentum carried by the flow.

meanings.short: The part of a fluid's stress that comes from friction between layers moving at different speeds.
meanings.long: It depends on the velocity gradients, through the shear and bulk viscosities. Added to the ideal-fluid stress it turns the Euler equation into the Navier–Stokes equation.

meanings.short: A force per unit area acting along a surface rather than straight across it, which tends to slide layers past each other.
meanings.long: A fluid at rest cannot hold a shear stress; that is what makes it a fluid. In a moving viscous fluid shear stress is proportional to how fast the speed changes across the layers.

meanings.short: The rule that along a streamline of a steady flow, pressure plus kinetic and potential energy per volume stays constant: faster fluid, lower pressure.
meanings.long: For an incompressible fluid, P + ½ρv² + ρgz is constant along each streamline. It explains why fluid speeds up and its pressure drops in a narrowing pipe, and how a Pitot tube measures speed. (Not the Bernoulli equation of differential equations, a different idea.)

meanings.short: A line that follows the direction of a fluid's velocity at every point; in a steady flow, the path each element takes.
meanings.long: Streamlines never cross. Where they crowd together the flow is fast, and where they spread apart it is slow.

meanings.short: A flow whose velocity, density and pressure at each fixed point do not change with time, though the fluid itself moves.
meanings.long: Water from a tap running at a constant rate is a steady flow. Each element follows a fixed streamline, which makes Bernoulli's equation especially useful.

meanings.short: A point in a flow where the fluid comes to rest, such as the front tip of a body facing the stream.
meanings.long: By Bernoulli's equation the pressure there is the highest on that streamline, which is how a Pitot tube measures speed.

meanings.short: A small tube facing into a flow that measures the flow's speed from the extra pressure where the fluid is brought to rest.
meanings.long: By Bernoulli's equation the pressure difference is ½ρv², so the speed follows. Aircraft use Pitot tubes to measure their airspeed.

meanings.short: The rule that a body in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it pushes aside.
meanings.long: The upward force comes from the pressure being larger lower down. A body floats when this buoyant force can balance its weight.

meanings.short: The height over which the pressure and density of an atmosphere fall by a factor e, about 2.7.
meanings.long: For an isothermal atmosphere it equals kT/mg, the thermal energy of a molecule divided by its weight. For the Earth's air it is about 8 km.

origin: Greek isos, equal, and therme, heat.

meanings.short: At one constant temperature throughout, or taking place without a change of temperature.
meanings.long: An isothermal atmosphere has the same temperature at every height, so its pressure falls exponentially. An isothermal process, such as a slow compression in contact with a heat bath, keeps the temperature fixed.

meanings.short: The carrying of heat by a moving fluid, as warm fluid rises and cool fluid sinks.
meanings.long: A fluid heated from below becomes unstable once the temperature difference is large enough, and starts to turn over in currents. Convection stirs the Earth's air, the oceans and the outer layers of the Sun.

meanings.short: A flow with no vorticity, whose velocity is the gradient of a single function, the velocity potential.
meanings.long: For an incompressible fluid the potential obeys Laplace's equation, so whole flows can be built by adding simple pieces such as uniform flow, sources and vortices. Pressure then follows from Bernoulli's equation.

meanings.short: The equation saying that the Laplacian of a function is zero everywhere, obeyed by potentials in regions with no sources.
meanings.long: It governs electric potentials in empty space, steady temperatures, and the velocity potential of incompressible potential flow. Its solutions have no maxima or minima inside the region.

meanings.short: A source concentrated at a single point, sending out light, fluid or field equally in all directions.
meanings.long: From a point source in three dimensions the flow or field spreads over spheres, so it falls off as one over the distance squared; in two dimensions it spreads over circles and falls off as one over the distance.

meanings.short: A flow with the same velocity everywhere, in speed and direction.
meanings.long: In potential flow it is the simplest building block, with a potential that grows steadily along the flow direction.

meanings.short: A flow round a line whose speed falls off as one over the distance, so it has no vorticity except on the line itself.
meanings.long: The circulation round any loop enclosing the line is the same. Bathtub drains and tornadoes look roughly like this away from their cores.

meanings.short: The thin layer of fluid next to a surface where viscosity slows the flow from its full speed to zero at the wall.
meanings.long: Outside the boundary layer the flow can often be treated as ideal. When the layer peels away from a body it leaves a wake and creates drag.

meanings.short: The region of slowed, often swirling fluid trailing behind a body moving through it.
meanings.long: Wakes come from viscosity: the boundary layer leaves the body and carries slowed fluid and eddies downstream. Ideal-fluid theory has no wakes, which is why it predicts no drag.

meanings.short: A measure of how hard a substance is to squeeze: the pressure increase needed per fractional decrease of its volume.
meanings.long: It equals ρ dP/dρ. The speed of sound is the square root of the bulk modulus divided by the density.

meanings.short: How fast small pressure waves travel through a material: about 340 metres per second in air, nearly 1500 in water.
meanings.long: It equals the square root of dP/dρ, the bulk modulus over the density. In an ideal gas it depends on the temperature but not the pressure.

meanings.short: A flow's speed divided by the speed of sound.
meanings.long: When the Mach number is small, density changes are tiny and a gas can be treated as incompressible. Above 1 the flow is supersonic and shock waves can form.

meanings.short: Faster than the speed of sound.
meanings.long: A supersonic body outruns the sound it makes, so the waves pile up into a cone-shaped shock wave behind it.

meanings.short: Slower than the speed of sound.
meanings.long: In subsonic flow, pressure changes can travel ahead of a moving body and warn the fluid in front, so no shock wave forms.

meanings.short: A very thin front across which pressure, density and temperature jump suddenly, formed when something moves faster than sound in a fluid.
meanings.long: Behind a supersonic body the shock forms a cone whose half-angle has sine equal to one over the Mach number. In astronomy, shocks heat gas falling into galaxies and exploding stars.

meanings.short: The loud bang heard on the ground when the shock wave of a supersonic aircraft sweeps past.
meanings.long: It is not a single event at the moment the aircraft passes the speed of sound: the shock cone travels with the aircraft and is heard wherever it passes.

meanings.short: Newton's second law for a viscous fluid: the Euler equation with an extra term for internal friction.
meanings.long: For an incompressible fluid the extra term is the kinematic viscosity times the Laplacian of the velocity. Whether its solutions always stay smooth is one of the great unsolved problems of mathematics.

meanings.short: The ordinary viscosity of a fluid: how much force per area it takes to slide its layers past each other at a given rate.
meanings.long: It is written η and measured in pascal seconds. Shear stress equals η times the rate at which the velocity changes across the flow.

meanings.short: A fluid's resistance to being squeezed or expanded quickly, as opposed to being sheared.
meanings.long: It matters only when the volume of fluid elements changes, so it plays no part in incompressible flow. It is written ζ.

meanings.short: A fluid's viscosity divided by its density, which sets how fast differences in speed spread through it.
meanings.long: It is written ν and measured in square metres per second, like a diffusion constant: velocity differences spread by diffusion with this constant.

meanings.short: The rule that a viscous fluid right next to a solid surface moves with the surface, with no sliding.
meanings.long: It is a boundary condition for the Navier–Stokes equation. Combined with viscosity it creates boundary layers and drag.

meanings.short: Smooth viscous flow through a round pipe, with the speed greatest on the axis and falling to zero at the wall.
meanings.long: The speed varies with radius as a parabola. The amount of fluid passing each second grows as the fourth power of the pipe's radius, so narrowing a pipe slightly cuts the flow a lot.

meanings.short: The amount of fluid passing through a pipe each second, counted as mass or volume.
meanings.long: For Poiseuille flow it grows as the fourth power of the pipe's radius and in proportion to the pressure drop per unit length.

meanings.short: A pure number, speed times size divided by kinematic viscosity, that compares inertia with viscosity in a flow.
meanings.long: At small Reynolds numbers viscosity wins and flow is smooth; at large ones inertia wins and flow tends to become turbulent. Two flows with the same Reynolds number and shape look alike, whatever their size.

meanings.short: Of a flow: smooth and orderly, with layers of fluid sliding past each other without mixing.
meanings.long: Flow is laminar when the Reynolds number is small. Above a critical value it usually becomes turbulent.

meanings.short: Very slow, very viscous flow, at a Reynolds number much less than 1, in which inertia can be ignored.
meanings.long: It obeys the linear Stokes equation, so flows can be added and reversed. Bacteria swimming and fine particles settling in water live in this world.

meanings.short: The Navier–Stokes equation with its inertia terms dropped, so that the pressure gradient just balances viscous friction.
meanings.long: It reads ∇P = η∇²v. Being linear, it can be solved exactly for a sphere, which gives Stokes' law for the drag.

meanings.short: The rule that the flux of a vector field's curl through a surface equals the field's line integral round the edge of that surface.
meanings.long: It turns an integral over a surface into one round its boundary curve. Green's theorem is its flat, two-dimensional case. In fluids it says the vorticity through a surface equals the circulation round its edge.

meanings.short: A measure of how stiff a material is when stretched: the pulling force per unit area divided by the fractional stretch it causes.
meanings.long: Steel has a Young's modulus of about 200 billion pascals, rubber only a few million. For a rod it plays the role that the spring constant plays for a spring.

meanings.short: Working out how a quantity must depend on others by making the units on both sides of an equation match.
meanings.long: It cannot give pure-number factors such as 2π, but it often gives the form of an answer with no detailed calculation. Kolmogorov's law of turbulence was found this way.

meanings.short: Pairs of coordinates and their momenta, treated as independent variables, in which the equations of motion take the form of Hamilton's equations.
meanings.long: Each coordinate q is paired with its canonical momentum p. A canonical transformation swaps one set of canonical variables for another, keeping Hamilton's equations valid.

meanings.short: The small resistance to a wheel or ball rolling on a surface, caused mainly by the surfaces bending slightly where they touch.
meanings.long: It is usually much weaker than sliding friction, which is why wheels are useful. It is modelled as a small force or torque against the rolling.

everyday: In everyday speech to lift is to raise something; in fluids lift is a force across the flow, not necessarily upwards.

meanings.short: The force a moving fluid exerts on a body across the flow, as on an aircraft wing; drag, by contrast, acts along the flow.
A stretch of slow motion left just after two fixed points have merged and vanished: the system crawls past where they were.
meanings.long: Just past a saddle-node bifurcation the rate of change is small but no longer zero, so the time spent there grows as one over the square root of the distance from the critical value.

everyday: In everyday speech a bottleneck is a narrow place where traffic slows; here it is a stretch of slow motion in time.
In everyday speech universal means found everywhere; here it means the same for a whole class of different systems.

meanings.short: The same for a whole class of different systems, whatever their details.
meanings.long: The Feigenbaum number is universal: many different maps and real systems show period doublings that crowd together at the same rate. Kolmogorov's law of turbulence is universal in the same way.

everyday: In everyday speech a map is a drawing of a place; in maths it is a rule that sends each point to another.

meanings.short: A rule that turns each state of a system into the next one, applied step by step, such as xₙ₊₁ = f(xₙ).
meanings.long: A map works in jumps rather than continuous time. A Poincaré section turns a flow into a map, and even a map of one variable, such as the logistic map, can be chaotic.

meanings.short: A rule that sends each point or object to another; a transformation.
A model of a galaxy or dark matter halo whose particles have the same spread of speeds everywhere; density falls as one over radius squared.
meanings.long: The name borrows from a gas at one temperature: equal spread of speeds plays the part of equal temperature. The singular version has no core and gives a flat rotation curve.
